title: Febrile Seizures
subject: Paediatrics
summary: A brief generalized tonic‑clonic event in a child 6 months‑5 years with fever and an obvious source, resolving quickly and not indicating epilepsy.

sections.p: A febrile seizure is a brief generalized tonic‑clonic event in a child 6 months‑5 years with fever, no prior epilepsy, and an identifiable source of infection.
All febrile seizures are considered simple unless they are prolonged, focal, or recur within 24 h. No formal staging beyond these criteria.
In low‑resource settings the leading infections are respiratory tract infections, malaria, and diarrhoeal disease. Other contributors include HIV, TB, and sickle cell crises.
The child has a sudden loss of consciousness, stiffening of limbs, and possible frothing at the mouth. The event lasts less than 15 min and the child recovers fully.
Investigations are guided by clinical suspicion of a serious underlying infection or metabolic disturbance.
Seizure lasting >15 min, focal features, or recurrence within 24 h warrants urgent evaluation for meningitis, encephalitis, or metabolic crisis.
Treat the underlying infection, provide supportive care, and monitor for recurrence. Antipyretics are used to reduce fever but are not seizure prophylaxis.
b: Give paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever
Start antibiotics if bacterial infection suspected

sections.p: Educate caregivers about fever management, vaccination, and when to seek care. No routine prophylaxis is recommended for simple febrile seizures.
Seizures due to meningitis, encephalitis, hypoglycaemia, or epilepsy may mimic febrile seizures but differ in duration, focality, and recurrence.
A normal CSF in early bacterial meningitis can occur; repeat lumbar puncture may be needed. Malaria parasitemia can be low in early infection.
b: False‑negative malaria rapid test in low parasitaemia

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of meningitis (neck stiffness, bulging fontanelle)

faq.q: Do febrile seizures increase the risk of epilepsy?
faq.a: A single simple febrile seizure does not increase epilepsy risk; recurrence raises the risk modestly.
No; antipyretics reduce fever but do not prevent seizures.

faq.q: What is the best first‑line antipyretic in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Paracetamol is preferred due to safety and availability.

exam: A 3‑year‑old presents with a brief generalized seizure during a fever; what is the next best step? — Assess for meningitis: check neck stiffness, perform lumbar puncture if indicated.

How would you differentiate a simple febrile seizure from a focal seizure? — Simple seizures are brief (<15 min), generalized, and non‑recurrent; focal seizures have focal onset, may last longer, and can recur.
Why is a rapid malaria test important in this setting? — Malaria can precipitate seizures; a positive test directs antimalarial therapy.
What is the management of a seizure lasting 20 min in a febrile child? — Treat as status epilepticus: give benzodiazepine, then antiepileptic if needed, and investigate for underlying cause.
When is an EEG indicated after a febrile seizure? — If the child has recurrent seizures or atypical features, to rule out epilepsy.
Why should you avoid giving phenobarbital as prophylaxis for simple febrile seizures? — It has no proven benefit and carries risk of sedation and hepatotoxicity.
